sentences.text: Here's a simple question: how many patients does each clinic have?
Our 103 patients are spread across four machines, in four piles.
Take Alder. It has 9 patients on this machine, 5 on this one, and 8 on each of the last two.
No machine can count Alder by itself. Alder's rows have to meet.
We could send every row to the driver and count there. For 103 rows, fine. For a whole registry, the driver chokes.
So Spark does something smarter: it moves rows sideways, between the machines.
Welcome to Spark, Visually.
Today: everyone sends to everyone.
Every Spark plan is cut wherever rows must change machines.
At each cut stands a wall: no work on the far side starts until all the work on the near side is done.
Today, we walk through that wall, and watch what crosses it.
On the far side of the wall, we'll have five reduce tasks. Five clinics, five reducers: one each, you'd hope.
So every pile gets sorted into five bins, one for each reducer.
Which bin? Spark turns the clinic's name into a big number, called a hash, and keeps the positive remainder after dividing by five.
The same name gives the same bin, on every machine. That's how Alder's rows will meet.
Now watch where the clinics go. Birch, bin 0. Alder, bin 1.
And Cedar, Dune and Elm all land in bin 4. Two bins get nothing at all.
A hash scatters keys. It doesn't deal them out evenly.
Each task writes its bins to its own machine's disk.
Notice that nothing has crossed the network yet.
So why the wall? Why can't a reducer start as soon as one pile is sorted?
Because every reducer needs a piece of every pile. Until the last pile is sorted, no reducer has all of its rows.
So the fastest machines wait for the slowest. Remember that wait. It comes back.
Now the second half. Each reducer visits every machine and fetches its bin.
Four piles and five reducers make 20 possible bins. Only 12 hold any rows, and only those 12 are fetched.
With our reducers placed like this, 9 of those bins cross the network: 79 of our 103 patients, on the move.
Now each clinic is in one place. Birch's 30 on one reducer, Alder's 30 on another, and 43 patients from three clinics, crowded onto a third.
And two reducers did nothing at all.
But to count patients, do we really need to move every patient?
Each machine can count its own pile first, and send just the numbers.
Now each machine sends one number per clinic: 20 small rows instead of 103.
On a cast this small, bytes barely fall, from 1,075 to 998, because every bin carries a fixed overhead.
Scale the cast up ten thousand times, and the count writes about 2,000 bytes instead of over a million.
Spark does this by itself. Its plan counts twice: a partial count before the wall, and a final count after it.
Not every question shrinks like that. Ask for the list of every patient's outcome, and every value still has to travel.
Still 20 rows, but each one carries a whole list, and the bytes climb to 1,502.
What if we ask for three reducers instead?
Alder, Birch and Elm all hash to the same one: 71 patients. Cedar and Dune share another: 32. The third gets nothing.
A stage ends when its busiest task ends. On real data, one crowded reducer can hold up a whole job.
And Spark's default is 200 reducers. For five clinics, that's 195 tasks with nothing to read.
Normally, adaptive execution sees that the bins are tiny, and merges them into a single task. We switched that off today, so you could see every bin.
Let's gather it up.
A shuffle sorts every pile into bins by key, and writes them to local disk.
Then a wall, and each reducer fetches its bin from every machine.
And Spark sends less when it can: partial results instead of every row.
Along the way, the hash put five clinics into three bins, and left two reducers idle.
Our code never said hash, or bins. We asked a question, and Spark chose how to answer it.
Next time: who makes that choice, and how.
This has been Spark, Visually. Thanks for watching the cluster with us.
